The baseline characteristics of the participants are shown in Table 1. A total of 770 (8.7%) of the participants were living with sarcopenia. The mean age of the participants was 39.2 years, and nearly half of the participants (50.4%) were female. A total of 36.8% of the participants were non-Hispanic white. The majority of the participants (83.5%) had a high school education or above, and more than half were married (59.7%). Figure 2 shows the differences in METs across different characteristics between the participants with and without sarcopenia. Total METs, METs for moderate-intensity PA, and METs for vigorous-intensity PA were significantly greater in the non-sarcopenia group than in the sarcopenia group (Fig. 2A-C). After stratification by occupation, the comparison of the METs for recreational PAs between sarcopenia patients and non-sarcopenia patients was similar to the results without stratification (Fig. 2G-I). However, there were no significant differences in total METs for occupational PA or METs for occupational vigorous-intensity PA across the groups of participants with and without sarcopenia (Fig. 2D and F). The cross-sectional associations between different intensities of PA (total, moderate, and vigorous) and sarcopenia are presented in Table 2. In the fully adjusted model, compared to participants without PAs (METs were 0), participants in the “low”, “moderate”, and “high” total METs groups had lower risks of sarcopenia (low: OR = 0.730, 95% CI: 0.583; 0.915, _p_ -value = 0.006; moderate: OR = 0.643, 95% CI: 0.485; 0.853, _p_ -value = 0.002; high: OR = 0.560; 95% CI: 0.457; 0.687, _p_ -value < 0.001). The stratified analysis of the associations between moderate- or vigorous-intensity METs and sarcopenia also yielded results similar to those of the non-stratified analysis. Table 3 shows the association between the intensity of occupational and recreational PA and sarcopenia. According to the fully adjusted model, the participants in the “high” total METs group had a significantly lower risk of sarcopenia (high: OR = 0.789; 95% CI = 0.653; 0.954; _p_ -value = 0.014). Similarly, “high” METs for moderate-intensity occupational PA were associated with a lower risk of sarcopenia (high: OR = 0.797, 95% CI: 0.649; 0.980, _p_ -value = 0.031); however, higher METs for vigorous-intensity occupational PA were not associated with sarcopenia compared to the reference group. A higher intensity of recreational PA was associated with a lower risk of sarcopenia, i.e., the participants who were labeled with “low”, “moderate” and “high” total METs for recreational PA had a decreased risk of sarcopenia (low: OR = 0.758, 95% CI: 0.623; 0.921, _p_ -value = 0.005; moderate: OR = 0.725, 95% CI: 0.553; 0.950, _p_ -value = 0.020; high: OR = 0.444, 95% CI: 0.327; 0.604, _p_ -value < 0.001) compared to the reference group. Figure 3 shows the dose-response relationships between different categories of PA intensity and sarcopenia. The relationships between total METs, vigorous-intensity METs and sarcopenia showed a nonlinear U-shaped trend (Fig. 3A and C). However, the relationship between moderate-intensity METs and sarcopenia revealed an L-shaped nonlinear trend. After stratifying PA by occupational and recreational type, the relationships between occupational moderate- and vigorousintensity PA and sarcopenia showed shapes similar to those of the unstratified relationship, whereas the nonlinear trend became nonsignificant (Fig. 3E and F). Forest plots were drawn to show the associations between different categories of PA intensity (i.e., total METs, occupational PA, recreational PA) and sarcopenia stratified by sex, ethnicity, education, marital status, and poverty status (Fig. 4). Stratified analysis revealed that male, education level of high school and above, and marital status were more likely to reduce the risk of sarcopenia at higher total METs for PA, as shown in Fig. 4A. According to the analysis of the association between occupational PA and sarcopenia, higher total METs for occupational PA did not reduce the risk of sarcopenia in most of the subgroups (Fig. 4B). However, higher total METs for recreational PA significantly decrease the risk of sarcopenia in many subgroups (Fig.4C). For example, married participants who were categorized as having “low”, “moderate” or “high” METs for recreational PA had a lower risk of sarcopenia than did the reference group (low: OR = 0.692, 95% CI: 0.540; 0.888, _p_ -value < 0.05; moderate: OR = 0.664, 95% CI: 0.470; 0.937, _p_ -value < 0.05; high: OR = 0.428, 95% CI: 0.287; 0.637, _p_ -value < 0.05). The results of the sensitivity analysis obtained from the imputed data were consistent with the results of the main analysis. The cross-sectional associations between different intensities of PA (total, moderate, and vigorous) and sarcopenia are presented in Supplemental Table 1. Compared to the participants without any PAs (METs were 0), the participants in the “low”, “moderate”, and “high” total MET groups had lower risks of sarcopenia (low: OR = 0.730, 95% CI: 0.583; 0.915, _p_ -value = 0.006; moderate: OR = 0.643, 95% CI: 0.485; 0.853, _p_ -value = 0.002; high: OR = 0.560, 95% CI: 0.457, 0.687; _p_ -value < 0.001). For moderate-intensity occupational PA, the “high” group had a lower risk of sarcopenia (high: OR = 0.797, 95% CI: 0.649; 0.980; _p_ -value = 0.031). Supplemental Fig. 1 shows the dose-response relationships between different categories of PA intensity and sarcopenia severity, which are consistent with the main analysis. The second method of sensitivity analysis, which included three categories of alcohol consumption (never, every day, and not every day) instead of the dichotomous variable (not drinking, drinking), also showed similar results (Supplemental Table 3). Compared to the participants without any PAs (METs were 0), the participants in the “moderate” and “high” total MET groups had lower risks of sarcopenia (moderate: OR = 0.639, 95% CI: 0.464; 0.881, _p_ -value < 0.01; high: OR = 0.579, 95% CI: 0.460; 0.728, _p_ -value < 0.001). Supplemental Table 4 shows the association between the intensity of occupational and recreational PA and sarcopenia. In the fully adjusted model, the participants in the “high” total occupational MET group had a significantly lower risk of sarcopenia (high: OR = 0.777, 95% CI: 0.631; 0.957; _p_ -value = 0.018). For moderate-intensity occupational PA, the “high” group had a lower risk of sarcopenia (high: OR = 0.757, 95% CI: 0.602; 0.952; _p_ -value = 0.017).
